root.stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the clinic because her attacks of cough, wheeze and chest tightness have become more frequent over 3 months, ever since she moved into an apartment with a roommate who smokes indoors. The attacks began in childhood, are worse in winter and after colds, and ease within minutes of her albuterol inhaler. She also coughs when she runs outside in cold weather and has had eczema since infancy. Tonight she has had 1 hour of wheezing and chest tightness. Her respirations are 28/min. Both inspiratory and expiratory wheezes are heard throughout the chest, the chest is hyperresonant with decreased tactile fremitus, and her heart sounds are normal without a click. She has no tremor, weight loss or leg swelling and no fever, and she coughs up only small amounts of thick, clear sputum. She has never smoked. Her blood eosinophil count is increased and her sputum contains many eosinophils.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Episodic, reversible narrowing of the airways set off by allergens, cold air, smoke and infections. The clincher: **recurrent attacks of wheeze, cough and chest tightness that ease with a bronchodilator and are normal in between**, with eczema and eosinophils.

nodes.q: Which test result confirms that her airflow limitation is reversible?
nodes.a: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) rises by at least 12% and 200 mL after an inhaled bronchodilator
nodes.note: Between attacks spirometry can be normal; a methacholine challenge then shows airways that narrow too easily. Peak flow also swings through the day.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity drives her allergic attacks?
nodes.note: Allergen cross-links immunoglobulin E (IgE) on mast cells, which release mediators within minutes (early phase) and again 4 to 8 hours later (late phase).

nodes.q: In the first exposure to an allergen, which sequence of events leads to IgE production?
nodes.a: T-lymphocyte induction, then cytokine release, then IgE production
nodes.note: A dendritic cell presents the allergen to a naive T cell, which becomes a T-helper 2 cell. It releases interleukin-4 and interleukin-13, which make B cells switch to IgE, and interleukin-5, which recruits eosinophils.

nodes.q: Which mast cell mediators are mainly responsible for the prolonged bronchoconstriction?
nodes.note: Histamine acts in the first minutes; the leukotrienes are the most potent bronchoconstrictors and also add mucus and edema, so they dominate the late phase.

nodes.q: Selective inhibition of which enzyme would most reduce the frequency of her attacks?
nodes.note: It makes leukotrienes from arachidonic acid. Zileuton blocks the enzyme; montelukast blocks the leukotriene D4 receptor instead. Cyclooxygenase inhibitors do not help.

nodes.q: Why can aspirin set off attacks in some people with asthma?
nodes.a: Cyclooxygenase is blocked, so arachidonic acid is shunted to the lipoxygenase pathway and more leukotrienes are made
nodes.note: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter triad): asthma, nasal polyps and attacks after aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Leukotriene blockers help.

nodes.q: Which product released by her eosinophils damages the airway lining?
nodes.note: Interleukin-5 draws eosinophils into the airway wall, where major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein strip the epithelium. Charcot-Leyden crystals (from eosinophil breakdown) can appear in sputum.

nodes.q: What are the long-term structural changes in her airway walls called?
nodes.note: Smooth muscle hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia with mucus plugs, and a thickened basement membrane (subepithelial fibrosis). Her sputum may show Curschmann spirals (twisted mucus casts of small airways) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (from eosinophil breakdown).

nodes.q: Which part of the airway is most prone to flow limitation from smooth muscle contraction?
nodes.note: Cartilage keeps the trachea and large bronchi open, and the alveoli have no smooth muscle, so the muscle bands of the small conducting airways narrow them most. Resistance rises and expiration is prolonged. A partial response to an inhaled bronchodilator leaves these small airways narrowed.

nodes.q: What makes her chest hyperresonant with decreased tactile fremitus?
nodes.note: Narrowed airways close early in expiration, so air stays in the lungs. Air-filled lung sounds hyperresonant and carries vibration poorly; consolidation does the opposite (dull note, increased fremitus).

nodes.q: Which blood gas pattern is expected early in her attack?
nodes.a: Low partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2) with a high pH (acute respiratory alkalosis)
nodes.note: Air hunger makes her hyperventilate, so minute ventilation rises above the normal 5 to 10 L/min and carbon dioxide is blown off. Typical values: PCO2 about 30 mm Hg, pH about 7.48, oxygen pressure normal or mildly low.

nodes.q: Which blood gas change warns that she is tiring and heading toward respiratory failure?
nodes.note: A normal PCO2 in someone who should be hyperventilating means the muscles are failing. Add a quiet chest, drowsiness or exhaustion and she needs intensive care.

nodes.q: What is an attack called when it does not respond to repeated bronchodilator doses?
nodes.note: Give oxygen, back-to-back inhaled albuterol with ipratropium and systemic corticosteroids; add intravenous magnesium sulfate if severe, and intubate if she tires.

nodes.q: Which kind of inhaled air most likely triggers her cough when she runs outside?
nodes.note: Fast breathing of cold, dry air cools and dries the airway lining, which sets off mast cell mediators and smooth muscle spasm (exercise-induced bronchoconstriction). Warm, humid air is the least likely trigger.

nodes.q: Her exercise symptoms could suggest other causes. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each of these can cause breathlessness on exertion, but only one gives wheeze and cough in attacks.

nodes.a: Ask the roommate not to smoke indoors
nodes.note: Tobacco smoke irritates the airway and is a proven trigger, so trigger avoidance comes first. Daily oral prednisone is not the next step for frequent attacks; a daily inhaled controller is.

nodes.q: Which drug class is the first-line daily controller for frequent attacks?
nodes.note: It lowers airway inflammation. A long-acting beta-2 agonist can be added but never used alone. Rinse the mouth afterwards to prevent oral thrush; oral prednisone is kept for severe exacerbations.

nodes.q: Which monoclonal antibody binds free immunoglobulin E (IgE) and is used for severe allergic asthma?
nodes.note: Less IgE is left to arm mast cells. Mepolizumab blocks interleukin-5 for severe eosinophilic asthma.

nodes.q: Which second messenger rises in her airway smooth muscle after albuterol?
nodes.note: Albuterol stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, which are Gs-coupled and activate adenylyl cyclase; the rise in cAMP relaxes airway smooth muscle.

nodes.q: Which effect is most likely to be seen after inhaled albuterol?
nodes.note: Beta-2 stimulation of skeletal muscle; fast pulse and a low potassium level can also occur. Inhaled albuterol is the preferred rescue drug in pregnancy too.

nodes.q: In some patients the same albuterol dose works less well even though blood levels are the same. Which mechanism most likely explains it?
nodes.a: A beta-2 receptor polymorphism with reduced signal transduction
nodes.note: The receptor gene has variants that blunt the cAMP response; because blood levels are normal, absorption and drug handling are not the problem. Receptor upregulation would make the drug work better.

nodes.note: The trap: both wheeze and both improve a little with bronchodilators.

nodes.q: Her sudden wheeze could suggest an inhaled foreign body. How do you tell them apart?

**Attacks since childhood with triggers and eosinophilia, a hyperresonant chest and normal heart sounds**

root.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 2 years of progressive shortness of breath on exertion, and last month she fainted while climbing stairs. Her ankles are swollen and her lips look bluish. She has lived at sea level all her life, has never smoked, and has no history of leg clots, sleep apnea, lung disease or heart disease. Her jugular veins are distended, a forceful systolic impulse is felt at the left lower sternal border, the second heart sound is loud over the pulmonic area, and the lungs are clear. Echocardiography shows a dilated, thick-walled right ventricle with normal left ventricular function and normal valves. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no mismatched defects, and pulmonary function tests are normal. Cardiac catheterization shows a high pulmonary artery pressure with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Narrowing and remodeling of the small pulmonary arteries that raises resistance in the lung circulation with no known cause. The clincher: **high pulmonary artery pressure with a normal wedge pressure and no lung, clot or left heart disease**, in a young woman with exertional breathlessness, fainting and right heart failure.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; exam options often use the older one.

nodes.q: In the World Health Organization classification, which group does her disease belong to?
nodes.note: Group 1 also includes heritable disease, drugs (amphetamines, old diet pills such as fenfluramine), connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis), human immunodeficiency virus infection and portal hypertension. Group 2 is left heart disease, group 3 lung disease or hypoxia, group 4 chronic clots, group 5 mixed causes.

nodes.q: Which catheterization finding separates it from pulmonary hypertension caused by left heart disease?
nodes.a: A normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (15 mm Hg or less) with high pulmonary vascular resistance
nodes.note: Mean pulmonary artery pressure is above 20 mm Hg at rest. The wedge pressure reflects left atrial pressure, so it is raised when the left heart is the cause.

nodes.q: Which test at catheterization picks out the few patients who can take calcium channel blockers?
nodes.a: Acute vasodilator testing (for example with inhaled nitric oxide)
nodes.note: Responders drop their mean pulmonary artery pressure by at least 10 mm Hg to below 40 mm Hg with output unchanged or higher; only a small minority respond.

nodes.q: Which heart sound finding reflects the high pressure in her pulmonary artery?
nodes.a: A loud pulmonic component (P2) of the second heart sound, louder than the aortic component (A2)
nodes.note: High pressure slams the pulmonary valve shut. Normally the aortic component is louder because the left side is the high-pressure system.

nodes.q: Which vasoconstrictor peptide is in excess in her small pulmonary arteries?
nodes.note: Endothelial injury tips the balance: too much endothelin-1, too little nitric oxide and prostacyclin, so the vessels constrict and their smooth muscle and endothelium overgrow.

nodes.q: Which gene is most often mutated in the heritable form?
nodes.note: Loss-of-function mutations, inherited as autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance; women are affected more often.

nodes.q: Which changes are seen in the small pulmonary arteries?
nodes.a: Medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis and plexiform lesions
nodes.note: Plexiform lesions are tangled, capillary-like channels formed in the narrowed arteries.

nodes.q: If she moved to high altitude, which response of her pulmonary arteries would raise the pressure further?
nodes.note: Low alveolar oxygen constricts pulmonary arteries (systemic arteries dilate instead), which normally diverts blood from poorly ventilated lung. Chronic hypoxia from altitude or lung disease remodels the vessels and causes World Health Organization group 3 pulmonary hypertension, then right ventricular hypertrophy.

nodes.q: Which oral drug blocks the receptors for this peptide?
nodes.note: An endothelin receptor antagonist (ambrisentan and macitentan are others). It is toxic to the liver and causes birth defects, so liver tests and pregnancy tests are needed.

nodes.q: Sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, lowers her pulmonary artery pressure by raising which intracellular molecule?
nodes.note: Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase to make cGMP, which relaxes the vessel smooth muscle; phosphodiesterase-5 breaks cGMP down, so blocking it keeps cGMP high. Do not combine with nitrates.

nodes.q: Which drug class replaces the lost vasodilator in the most severe disease?
nodes.note: Given by continuous infusion or inhalation; they also reduce platelet clumping. Flushing, jaw pain and diarrhea are common.

nodes.q: Which load on her heart rises and makes her cardiac output fall?
nodes.note: The right ventricle pumps against high resistance, thickens, then dilates and fails. Less blood reaches the left heart, so left ventricular preload and cardiac output fall.

nodes.q: Which condition follows when the right ventricle fails because of lung vessel disease?
nodes.note: Distended neck veins, ankle edema and an enlarged, tender liver.

nodes.q: Why does she faint when climbing stairs?
nodes.a: The right ventricle cannot raise its output against fixed high resistance, so the brain is under-perfused
nodes.note: Fainting on exertion marks severe disease; sudden death from arrhythmia or right heart failure is the usual end.

nodes.q: Which test screens for it and shows the right ventricle?
nodes.note: It shows right ventricular dilation and thickening and estimates the pulmonary pressure from the tricuspid regurgitant jet. Right heart catheterization is still needed to confirm.

nodes.q: Her pulmonary hypertension could instead come from years of living at high altitude. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Years at high altitude with chronic low oxygen**; improves with descent or oxygen; right heart strain follows
**Sea-level life with normal oxygen levels and no lung, clot or left heart disease**

nodes.note: Both end in a thick, failing right ventricle; at altitude the cause is hypoxic vasoconstriction (group 3).

nodes.q: Her normal wedge pressure could also fit chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Old, unresolved clots: ventilation-perfusion scan with mismatched segmental defects**, often after a pulmonary embolism
**Normal ventilation-perfusion scan**, no history of leg clots

nodes.note: The trap: both give high pulmonary pressure with a normal wedge pressure. The clot form is curable with surgical removal of the clots (pulmonary thromboendarterectomy) plus lifelong anticoagulation, so the scan is never skipped.

nodes.q: Her breathlessness and swollen ankles could come from left heart failure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised wedge pressure**, orthopnea, basal crackles, and left ventricular or mitral valve disease on echocardiography
**Normal wedge pressure**, clear lungs, normal left ventricle and valves

nodes.q: Lung disease was also a possible cause. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Chronic lung disease is the usual cause of group 3 pulmonary hypertension.

root.stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department in January after 2 days of runny nose, cough and a low-grade fever, followed by fast breathing and noisy wheezing that make feeding difficult. He was born at term, this is his first wheezing illness, and his older brother has a cold. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 140/min and respirations are 56/min. Intercostal retractions and nasal flaring are present, wheezes and fine crackles are heard in all lung fields, and there is no stridor or barking cough. There are no skin vesicles. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with patchy atelectasis. A virus isolated from his nasal secretions causes multinucleated giant cells in cell culture. A blood culture grows coagulase-negative, catalase-positive gram-positive cocci in clusters in one of two bottles; he has no indwelling catheter.

highlight: runny nose, cough and a low-grade fever
multinucleated giant cells in cell culture
coagulase-negative, catalase-positive gram-positive cocci in clusters in one of two bottles

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A viral infection of the small airways in infants under 2 years, peaking in winter. The clincher: **a runny nose and cough followed by wheeze, fast breathing and retractions in a young infant in winter**. It is the commonest cause of bronchiolitis and of pneumonia in infants; it spreads by droplets and contaminated hands and surfaces.

nodes.q: Which virus family is it classically grouped in?
nodes.note: An enveloped, nonsegmented, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus.

nodes.q: Which feature in cell culture gave the virus its name?
nodes.a: Syncytia: infected cells fuse into multinucleated giant cells
nodes.note: The same fusion spreads infection from cell to cell in the airway lining.

nodes.q: Which viral surface protein causes this fusion and lets the virus enter cells?
nodes.note: Parainfluenza and measles viruses also fuse cells, but the F protein of RSV is the main target for prevention.

nodes.q: Which monoclonal antibody, given to high-risk infants during the season, targets that protein?
nodes.note: Nirsevimab is a longer-acting antibody against the same protein, and a vaccine given in late pregnancy also protects newborns.

nodes.q: Which part of the airway is inflamed and blocked?
nodes.note: Epithelial necrosis, edema and mucus plugs block the narrow small airways, which causes air trapping (hyperinflation) and patchy collapse.

nodes.q: Which organism does the blood culture result represent?
nodes.note: Catalase positive means a staphylococcus, coagulase negative rules out Staphylococcus aureus. It is normal skin flora.

nodes.q: What is the most likely meaning of that result in one of two bottles in a child with no catheter?
nodes.a: Contamination with skin flora, not the cause of the illness
nodes.note: Think of it as real only if several bottles grow it, or a catheter or prosthetic material is present (it forms a biofilm). Bronchiolitis itself is viral.

nodes.q: What is the main treatment?
nodes.a: Supportive care: oxygen, fluids and nasal suction
nodes.note: Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are not used routinely. Admit for low oxygen, apnea or poor feeding.

nodes.q: Which antiviral guanosine analogue, which blocks viral RNA synthesis, is kept for severe disease or weak immunity?
nodes.note: It inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, lowering guanosine triphosphate. Given by aerosol; it can cause hemolytic anemia and is teratogenic. Acyclovir (herpes) and amantadine (influenza A) have no effect on this virus.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening event can be the first sign in the youngest infants?
nodes.note: Most common in infants under 2 months and in premature babies, so they are monitored closely.

nodes.q: Which chronic airway problem is more likely in these children later?
nodes.note: The link with later asthma is well described, although whether the infection causes it is still debated.

nodes.q: His noisy breathing could suggest croup. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Age 6 months to 3 years. **Barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor**, with a steeple sign on x-ray
Under 2 years. **Wheezes, fine crackles and retractions with no stridor or barking cough**

nodes.q: His wheeze could suggest asthma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older child with **recurrent episodes, eczema or allergies, and relief with albuterol**
**First wheezing illness in an infant under 2 with a cold in winter**; little response to bronchodilators

nodes.note: The trap: both wheeze, and a baby with bronchiolitis may wheeze again later.

nodes.q: Other causes of cough and fast breathing were also possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each has a different clincher.

root.stem: A 63-year-old woman has had a 3-month cough with blood-streaked sputum and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. For 2 weeks her face and neck have been swelling, worse in the morning and when she bends forward. She has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 42 years. She lives in an older house and spends most evenings in the basement family room. She takes enalapril for hypertension. Her fingertips are rounded with curved nails, her wrists and ankles are painful and swollen, and x-rays of the hands show new bone formation along the shafts of the metacarpals. Her face and neck are swollen with distended neck veins and prominent veins over the upper chest, and breath sounds are slightly decreased. She has no tremor, muscle cramps or tongue swelling, and no jaundice, cyanosis or dry crackles at the lung bases. Her serum sodium concentration is 125 mEq/L.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A malignant tumor of the airway lining or lung tissue. The clincher: **a long-term heavy smoker with blood-streaked sputum and weight loss, plus tumor complications: face and neck swelling with distended veins, clubbing with bone pain, and low sodium**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; exam options often use the second.

nodes.q: Which exposure causes most cases?
nodes.note: Risk rises with the number of pack-years; smoking causes roughly 80 to 90% of cases.

nodes.q: Apart from smoking, which exposure in her home raises her risk?
nodes.a: Radon gas collecting in the basement
nodes.note: Radon seeps from soil and concentrates in basements; it is the second leading cause of lung cancer and the leading cause in never-smokers. Its decay products give off alpha particles that damage airway cell DNA. Wood dust is tied mainly to cancers of the nose and sinuses.

nodes.q: Which histologic type is the most common overall?
nodes.note: Usually peripheral, and the type seen most in women and never-smokers. Squamous cell carcinoma is central and cavitates; small cell carcinoma is central and neuroendocrine.

nodes.q: Which paraneoplastic syndrome explains her serum sodium of 125 mEq/L?
nodes.a: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
nodes.note: The tumor makes antidiuretic hormone, so the body keeps water, the blood is diluted, and the urine stays concentrated. Treatment is fluid restriction.

nodes.q: Which type of lung cancer classically makes the hormone behind this syndrome?
nodes.note: A central tumor of neuroendocrine cells; it can also make adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH, causing Cushing syndrome) and cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome. It is treated with chemotherapy and radiation, not surgery.

nodes.q: Which type of lung cancer most often raises serum calcium by secreting parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP)?
nodes.note: A central tumor of smokers that may cavitate; keratin pearls and intercellular bridges on histology.

nodes.q: Which complication explains the swelling of her face and neck with distended neck veins?
nodes.note: The tumor or its lymph nodes compress the thin-walled SVC, so blood from the head, neck and arms cannot drain. Swelling is worse in the morning and on bending forward, and collateral veins appear on the chest wall.

nodes.q: Which treatment relieves the obstruction?
nodes.a: Treatment of the tumor with radiation or chemotherapy, with an SVC stent when severe
nodes.note: Raise the head of the bed; airway swelling or brain edema makes it an emergency.

nodes.q: Which paraneoplastic syndrome explains the clubbing with painful swollen wrists and ankles and new bone on x-ray?
nodes.note: New bone is laid down under the periosteum of long bones (tibia, radius, metacarpals) with arthritis of nearby joints. It fades after the tumor is removed.

nodes.q: Other diseases cause clubbing or swollen joints. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: All can cause clubbing, but only one gives new bone along the shafts with a smoking-related tumor.

nodes.q: A tumor at the lung apex can press on the sympathetic chain. Which syndrome follows?
nodes.note: Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on the same side, with shoulder and arm pain from the C8 to T1 roots.

nodes.q: Which organs does it most often spread to?
nodes.a: Brain, bone, liver and adrenal glands
nodes.note: Brain metastases bring headaches and seizures; bone metastases bring pain and fractures. Overall, the most common tumor found in the lung is a metastasis from elsewhere, not a primary lung cancer.

nodes.q: Which test screens high-risk patients?
nodes.note: For ages 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years.

nodes.q: Which test establishes the type of tumor?
nodes.a: Biopsy (bronchoscopy or needle guided by CT) with histology
nodes.note: Then stage with positron emission tomography (PET) combined with CT, sampling of mediastinal nodes and brain magnetic resonance imaging.

nodes.q: Which treatment fits a localized non-small cell tumor?

nodes.q: Why are tactile fremitus and breath sounds reduced over the right chest while the percussion note is booming?

nodes.note: Air between the lung and the chest wall damps sound and vibration, unlike consolidated lung, which conducts them better. The trachea stays midline unless the air is under tension.

nodes.q: Which acid-base disorder does his blood gas show?
nodes.note: Pain and hypoxemia drive fast breathing, so carbon dioxide is blown off. The alveolar-arterial gradient is wide because the collapsed lung is perfused but not ventilated.

nodes.note: Give oxygen. A small, stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax can be watched with oxygen, or a larger one treated by needle aspiration.

nodes.q: What happens to the upper airway during sleep?
nodes.a: Pharyngeal muscle tone falls and the soft tissues of the throat collapse the airway
nodes.note: Fat around the neck and a large tongue add to the collapse. The chest and abdomen keep trying to breathe against the closed airway, and the person briefly wakes, which breaks up sleep.

nodes.q: In which sleep stage are the airway collapses usually longest?
nodes.note: Muscle tone is lowest in REM sleep, including the throat muscles, so the airway collapses most easily.

nodes.q: Which test confirms it?
nodes.note: The apnea-hypopnea index counts pauses and partial pauses per hour of sleep; 5 or more with symptoms, or 15 or more without symptoms, makes the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which lung vessel reaction to the low oxygen raises the pressure in the pulmonary artery?

nodes.q: What is his hematocrit of 54% called?

nodes.q: Which cardiovascular risk factor does the repeated nocturnal arousal produce?

nodes.note: Surges of sympathetic activity at each apnea raise the pressure. Obstructive sleep apnea is a recognized secondary cause of hypertension. Long-term positive airway pressure lowers blood pressure; it does not lower glucose, uric acid or creatinine.

nodes.q: Which treatment is first-line for moderate to severe disease?

nodes.q: How does nightly positive airway pressure (CPAP or bilevel) help him?
nodes.a: It splints the airway open during sleep so ventilation continues
nodes.note: Bilevel positive airway pressure gives a higher pressure on inspiration than on expiration; it is used when CPAP is not tolerated or when hypoventilation is present.

nodes.q: His pauses in airflow could suggest central sleep apnea. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A high-grade neuroendocrine tumor of heavy smokers. The clincher: **central hilar mass of small round blue cells that stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin, with paraneoplastic syndromes and early spread**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same tumor, named for the oat-shaped cells; small cell lung cancer is a third wording.

nodes.q: Which cells does it arise from?
nodes.a: Neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells of the bronchial mucosa
nodes.note: The cells are small with scant cytoplasm, molded nuclei and crush artifact. They carry neurosecretory granules, which explains hormone secretion.

nodes.q: Which two tumor suppressor genes are most often lost?
nodes.note: Amplification of MYC is also common.

nodes.q: Which mediators released by the tumor and host cells most likely explain the weight loss and poor appetite?

nodes.q: Which hormone made by the tumor lowers his sodium?
nodes.note: This is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). The patient is clinically euvolemic and may gain a little weight from retained water.

nodes.q: Which urine sodium and serum osmolality pattern is expected?
nodes.a: Raised urine sodium (above 40 mEq/L) with low serum osmolality

nodes.q: How is the low sodium treated in a stable patient?

nodes.q: Which paraneoplastic neuromuscular syndrome causes proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort?
nodes.note: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release; repeated effort builds up calcium and strength. Dry mouth is common.

nodes.q: Which other hormone can the tumor make, causing Cushing syndrome with low potassium?
nodes.note: Ectopic hormone production is typical of small cell carcinoma, unlike squamous cell carcinoma, which makes parathyroid hormone-related peptide.

nodes.q: If his hilar mass grows into the mediastinum and compresses the vein draining the head and arms, which syndrome results?
nodes.note: Facial and arm swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins and a raised jugular venous pressure. It causes swelling, not weight loss.

nodes.q: What does his single frontal lobe mass with edema most likely represent?

nodes.q: Which radiation is given to prevent brain spread in selected patients who respond to treatment?

nodes.q: Which treatment is used because the tumor has spread beyond one hemithorax?

nodes.q: Which enzyme does etoposide inhibit?

nodes.a: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
nodes.note: A non-small cell lung cancer of heavy smokers that grows in the central airways. The clincher: **a central hilar mass in a smoker with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges on biopsy, often with hypercalcemia and a suppressed parathyroid hormone**.

nodes.note: An adaptive, reversible change after chronic injury from smoke; it is not yet cancer and can reverse if he stops smoking.

nodes.q: If the smoke exposure continues, which two steps lead on to this cancer?
nodes.note: Dysplasia (disordered, atypical cells, still reversible early) is followed by carcinoma in situ (atypia through the full thickness, basement membrane intact); invasive carcinoma breaks through the basement membrane.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A slow-growing, strictly aerobic bacillus with a waxy cell wall, so it is acid-fast. Its love of oxygen explains the upper-lobe preference.

nodes.q: His first infection, years ago, most likely left a small scar in the lower part of the lung plus a calcified hilar lymph node. What is that pair called?
nodes.note: Primary tuberculosis: the bacilli settle in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe (Ghon focus) and drain to hilar nodes. Most heal and stay latent. Reactivation favours the apex, where oxygen is highest.

nodes.q: What does the lung biopsy show?
nodes.a: Caseating granulomas: epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells around central caseous necrosis
nodes.note: Caseation means a cheese-like, structureless centre. Fungal infections such as histoplasmosis can also caseate; sarcoidosis does not.

nodes.q: Which T-cell cytokine activates macrophages to wall off the bacilli?
nodes.note: Made by T helper 1 cells; it activates macrophages to kill the bacteria and form granulomas.

nodes.q: Which macrophage cytokine in turn activates the T helper 1 cells, completing the loop?
nodes.note: The reciprocal activation: infected macrophages release IL-12, T helper 1 cells release interferon-gamma. Defects in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway cause severe mycobacterial infection.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity causes the tissue destruction and the skin test reaction?
nodes.note: T cell-mediated, not antibody-mediated; the injury comes from activated macrophages and their enzymes.

nodes.q: At 48 hours, which cell predominates in his area of skin induration?
nodes.note: The skin test is a type IV reaction read at 48 to 72 hours. A positive test means exposure; it cannot tell latent infection from active disease.

nodes.q: Which immune function did infliximab impair, allowing the old infection to reactivate?
nodes.note: Granulomas wall off the bacilli in latent infection; without them the bacilli escape and the infection reactivates.

nodes.q: Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody against which cytokine?
nodes.note: Released by macrophages and needed to keep granulomas intact. Latent infection must be looked for before starting any drug of this class.

nodes.q: Which test should have been done before he started a TNF-alpha inhibitor?
nodes.a: Screening for latent tuberculosis with a tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay
nodes.note: Latent infection is treated first (for example with isoniazid), and the biologic is started afterwards.

nodes.q: Most infected people never become ill. What is that state called?
nodes.note: Positive skin test, no symptoms, normal chest x-ray and not contagious. About 5-10% reactivate over a lifetime, mainly with weak T-cell immunity.

nodes.q: Suppose the bacilli now enter his bloodstream. What pattern of disease results?
nodes.note: Countless millet-seed-sized granulomas in the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, adrenals, meninges and bone marrow. Spread to the spine gives Pott disease (vertebral osteomyelitis); spread to the meninges gives basal meningitis, the deadliest form. Weak T-cell immunity, as on infliximab, raises the risk.

nodes.q: What is the standard drug regimen?
nodes.a: Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then rifampin and isoniazid for 4 months
nodes.note: Four drugs are needed to prevent resistance.

nodes.q: Which bacterial enzyme does rifampin inhibit?
nodes.note: It blocks transcription so no mRNA, and therefore no protein, is made. Rifampin also induces cytochrome P450 and colours body fluids orange.

nodes.q: Which vitamin is given with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy?
nodes.note: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine; it also causes hepatitis and, in slow acetylators, more toxicity.

nodes.q: His upper-lobe lesions and granulomas could suggest sarcoidosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, raised angiotensin-converting enzyme**, often a young African American woman; no cavity and no acid-fast bacilli
**Caseating granulomas, acid-fast bacilli, cavity at the apex, fever and night sweats**

nodes.note: The trap: both form granulomas in the lungs, and both can cause fever, cough and weight loss.

nodes.q: A cavity with caseating granulomas could be histoplasmosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, bat or bird droppings and caves; small yeasts inside macrophages**
**Acid-fast bacilli in a city-dweller with no cave exposure**

nodes.q: His weight loss, bloody sputum and upper-lobe lesion could suggest lung cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Smoker with a mass; cancer cells on biopsy; no fever or night sweats**
**Never smoked; fever and night sweats with acid-fast bacilli and caseating granulomas**

root.stem: A 42-year-old man is admitted with peritonitis from a perforated appendix, and blood cultures grow gram-negative rods. One day after surgery he becomes severely short of breath with a respiratory rate of 34/min and diffuse crackles. Arterial oxygen is 55 mm Hg on 60% oxygen. Chest x-ray shows fluffy bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mm Hg. He has no leg swelling, no third heart sound and no sudden chest pain. He is intubated and ventilated with 90% oxygen at a low tidal volume.
root.oneliner: 42M + peritonitis with gram-negative sepsis + severe dyspnea, rate 34, crackles + PaO2 55 on 60% oxygen + bilateral fluffy infiltrates, normal heart size + wedge pressure 10 + no leg swelling, no S3, no sudden chest pain + ventilated on 90% oxygen at low tidal volume
highlight: Arterial oxygen is 55 mm Hg on 60% oxygen
fluffy bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size
pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mm Hg
no leg swelling, no third heart sound and no sudden chest pain
ventilated with 90% oxygen at a low tidal volume

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Sudden, severe, non-cardiogenic lung failure after a trigger. The clincher: **severe hypoxemia within a week of sepsis, burns, trauma or pancreatitis, with bilateral infiltrates and a normal wedge pressure**.

nodes.q: Which condition set off the lung injury in him?
nodes.note: Sepsis is the commonest cause. Other classic triggers: severe burns, major trauma, aspiration of gastric contents, acute pancreatitis, transfusion and smoke inhalation.

nodes.q: Which ratio grades the severity of his hypoxemia?
nodes.a: Arterial oxygen pressure divided by inspired oxygen fraction (PaO2/FiO2); his is about 92, which is severe
nodes.note: Within 1 week of a trigger, bilateral opacities not explained by heart failure, and a ratio of 300 or less (mild 201-300, moderate 101-200, severe 100 or less) on positive end-expiratory pressure of at least 5 cm H2O.

nodes.q: Which two layers of the alveolar wall are injured?
nodes.note: Damage to the blood-air barrier lets fluid and protein pour into the air spaces; surfactant is also lost.

nodes.q: Which white blood cell, drawn into the lung by interleukin-8, does most of the damage?
nodes.note: Macrophages activated through Toll-like receptors and nuclear factor-kappa B release tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1 and interleukin-8; neutrophils then release proteases and oxygen radicals that break the barrier.

nodes.q: Which anti-inflammatory cytokine, if raised, would limit the injury?
nodes.note: It shuts down macrophage and T-cell cytokine release. Raising the pro-inflammatory mediators makes the damage worse.

nodes.q: Which mechanism causes his low arterial oxygen?
nodes.a: Leak of protein-rich fluid from injured capillaries into the alveoli (non-cardiogenic edema), causing a shunt
nodes.note: Perfused but fluid-filled alveoli cannot oxygenate blood, so oxygen alone corrects little (a shunt). Lungs are stiff and heavy.

nodes.q: What does the lung show under the microscope at autopsy?
nodes.a: Hyaline membranes lining the alveoli, with widened alveolar septa
nodes.note: Pink bands of dead cells, fibrin and proteins on the alveolar walls; lungs are firm, red and heavy.

nodes.q: What name does the pathologist give to this pattern of lung injury?
nodes.note: The microscopic picture of ARDS. Older exam names for the syndrome: shock lung and adult respiratory distress syndrome.

nodes.q: If he recovered, which cell would multiply to rebuild the alveolar lining?
nodes.note: Type I pneumocytes die; type II cells divide and differentiate into new type I cells.

nodes.q: Which measurement shows the edema is not from the left heart?
nodes.a: A normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (18 mm Hg or less)
nodes.note: Equivalent: echocardiography with normal left ventricular function.

nodes.q: Which ventilator strategy lowers mortality?
nodes.a: Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg of ideal body weight) with positive end-expiratory pressure
nodes.note: Plateau pressure below 30 cm H2O; prone positioning helps severe cases. Avoids stretch injury to open alveoli.

nodes.q: Breathing 90% oxygen for hours can collapse alveoli behind blocked airways. What is this called?
nodes.note: Oxygen is absorbed faster than nitrogen can replace it, so poorly ventilated alveoli collapse. Prolonged high oxygen also causes oxygen toxicity from free radicals.

nodes.q: Weeks later, which lung change can follow in survivors?
nodes.note: The healing phase after the exudative stage; survivors can have restrictive disease.

nodes.q: His crackles and fluffy infiltrates could be cardiogenic pulmonary edema. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High wedge pressure, third heart sound (S3), enlarged heart, raised B-type natriuretic peptide, quick response to diuretics**
**Normal wedge pressure, normal heart size and a systemic trigger (sepsis)**; no response to diuretics

nodes.note: The trap: both give bilateral infiltrates and hypoxemia.

nodes.q: Hyaline membranes also line the alveoli of premature babies with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Premature newborn with too little surfactant, low lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio, ground-glass lungs**; hyaline membranes too
**Adult with sepsis or another trigger; surfactant was normal until the injury**; damage to the alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium

nodes.note: Both show hyaline membranes, but the cause differs: surfactant deficiency versus injury.

nodes.q: His sudden hypoxemia could be pulmonary embolism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Leg swelling or recent immobility, pleuritic chest pain; clear lung fields on x-ray, wedge pressure normal**
**Bilateral fluffy infiltrates with crackles and sepsis**; no calf swelling or pain

nodes.q: His fever and crackles could be simple pneumonia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Focal consolidation, productive cough**; improves with antibiotics
**Diffuse bilateral infiltrates with refractory hypoxemia requiring high oxygen**

root.stem: A 47-year-old man has had 5 days of dry cough and increasing shortness of breath. He received a kidney transplant 6 weeks ago and takes cyclosporine and prednisone. His temperature is 38.3 C and oxygen saturation is 87% on room air. Chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Transbronchial biopsy shows enlarged cells with large intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo; a silver stain shows no cysts, there are no fungal hyphae, and his serum creatinine is unchanged. His lactate dehydrogenase is normal and he has no known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.
root.oneliner: 47M + kidney transplant 6 weeks ago on cyclosporine and prednisone + 5 days of dry cough and dyspnea + fever, saturation 87% + diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates + enlarged cells with intranuclear inclusions and clear halo + silver stain negative, no hyphae + unchanged creatinine + normal LDH, no HIV
highlight: intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo
a silver stain shows no cysts
no known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A viral lung infection of immunosuppressed hosts, usually 1 to 4 months after transplant. The clincher: **enlarged cells with an owl-eye intranuclear inclusion on lung biopsy**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease; exam options use either word.

nodes.q: Which biopsy finding clinches the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Enlarged cells with an 'owl-eye' intranuclear inclusion
nodes.note: Large basophilic intranuclear inclusion with a clear halo; cytoplasmic inclusions can also be seen.

nodes.q: Which family of viruses does CMV belong to?
nodes.note: A double-stranded DNA virus that stays latent after the first infection.

nodes.q: In which cells does CMV lie latent?
nodes.a: Mononuclear white blood cells (monocytes) and their precursors
nodes.note: Reactivation when T-cell immunity falls; it can also be transmitted by the transplanted organ.

nodes.q: Which donor-recipient pairing carries the highest risk of this infection after transplant?
nodes.a: A CMV-seropositive donor and a CMV-seronegative recipient
nodes.note: The latent virus arrives inside the graft in a recipient with no immunity. These patients get valganciclovir prophylaxis.

nodes.q: Cyclosporine makes reactivation possible. Which cells does it impair?
nodes.note: It inhibits calcineurin, so T cells cannot make interleukin-2. Without cytotoxic T cells the virus reactivates.

nodes.q: Besides transplant recipients, which group of patients gets this lung infection once their CD4 T-cell count falls below about 50 per microliter?
nodes.a: Patients with advanced HIV infection (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, AIDS)
nodes.note: In AIDS, CMV more often causes retinitis, colitis and esophagitis, but it can also infect the lung. Bone marrow transplant recipients with graft-versus-host disease are another high-risk group.

nodes.q: Which lung injury pattern explains his low oxygen?
nodes.a: Diffuse alveolar damage, with interstitial inflammation thickening the alveolar walls
nodes.note: Fluid and inflammation slow gas exchange across the thickened barrier.

nodes.q: Which blood test shows active infection and its load?
nodes.a: Quantitative CMV DNA polymerase chain reaction
nodes.note: Biopsy shows tissue disease; a positive antibody (IgG) only shows past infection.

nodes.q: Which antiviral drug treats it?
nodes.note: Foscarnet if resistance develops; neutropenia is the main toxicity of ganciclovir.

nodes.q: Which viral enzyme does ganciclovir ultimately block?
nodes.note: Ganciclovir is phosphorylated by a viral kinase (UL97) and then inhibits DNA polymerase. Foscarnet blocks the enzyme directly and needs no activation.

nodes.q: His interstitial infiltrates could be Pneumocystis pneumonia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Silver stain shows cysts; high lactate dehydrogenase; ground-glass lungs in advanced HIV infection (CD4 below 200)**; prevented by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
**Owl-eye intranuclear inclusions; silver stain negative**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause diffuse infiltrates and hypoxemia in an immunosuppressed host.

nodes.q: His immunosuppression could suggest aspergillosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hyphae branching at acute angles that invade vessels; nodules with a halo, infarcts, neutropenia**
**Viral inclusions and no hyphae**; diffuse interstitial pattern

nodes.q: His hypoxemia could be from acute rejection of the graft. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rising creatinine and a graft biopsy with lymphocytic infiltration of the transplanted organ**
**Normal creatinine; the lung biopsy shows viral inclusions**

nodes.q: Infection after a transplant could also come from Epstein-Barr virus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Masses or nodules of proliferating B lymphocytes, usually months to years after transplant**; no intranuclear inclusions
**Diffuse interstitial infiltrates 1 to 4 months after transplant with owl-eye inclusions**

root.stem: A 52-year-old woman with breast cancer completed a 4-week course of chest radiation 6 months ago. She now has a dry cough and shortness of breath with a respiratory rate of 26/min. She is afebrile. Examination shows no recurrence of the cancer and no mass. CT of the chest shows bilateral patches of volume loss in the upper lung fields with linear scarring, but the airways are open and there is no pleural fluid.
root.oneliner: 52F + breast cancer + 4-week chest radiation course 6 months ago + dry cough, dyspnea, rate 26 + afebrile + no recurrence or mass + patchy upper-field volume loss with scarring + open airways, no pleural fluid
highlight: 4-week course of chest radiation 6 months ago
no recurrence of the cancer and no mass
bilateral patches of volume loss in the upper lung fields
airways are open and there is no pleural fluid

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Scarring of lung tissue inside the radiation field. The clincher: **volume loss and scarring in the upper lungs 6 or more months after chest radiation, with open airways and no mass**.

nodes.q: Which cells does radiation injure first?
nodes.a: Type II pneumocytes and capillary endothelial cells
nodes.note: Free radicals damage DNA, causing cell death and leaking capillaries.

nodes.q: Which cells then lay down the collagen that scars the lung?
nodes.a: Fibroblasts, driven by transforming growth factor-beta
nodes.note: Chronic injury leads to collagen deposition and loss of the alveolar architecture.

nodes.q: What acute inflammatory phase comes 1 to 3 months after radiation, before the scarring?
nodes.note: Fever, cough and infiltrates limited to the radiation field; steroids help. Fibrosis follows after about 6 months.

nodes.q: Which type of atelectasis explains her patches of volume loss?
nodes.a: Contraction (cicatrization) atelectasis: scar tissue shrinks the lung so it cannot expand
nodes.note: The other types: resorption (blocked airway), compression (pleural fluid or air) and patchy atelectasis from loss of surfactant.

nodes.q: Which pulmonary function pattern follows?
nodes.a: Restrictive pattern with a low diffusing capacity
nodes.note: Low total lung capacity and forced vital capacity with a normal or high ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity; the low diffusing capacity shows the damaged alveolar-capillary barrier.

nodes.q: What is given for the early inflammatory phase?
nodes.note: Established fibrosis does not reverse; treatment is supportive with oxygen as needed.

nodes.q: Her lung collapse could be resorption atelectasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A blocked bronchus (mucus plug, tumor or foreign body)**; the lobe collapses and the mediastinum shifts toward the collapse
**Open airways with scarring after radiation or fibrosis**; patchy and limited to the field

nodes.note: The trap: both cause lung collapse.

nodes.q: Her volume loss could be compression atelectasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pleural effusion or pneumothorax pushing on the lung**; the mediastinum may shift away
**No pleural fluid or air; scarring within the radiation field**

nodes.q: Her scarring could be recurrent cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **New mass, lymphangitic spread or a nodule that grows**
**No mass; scarring that follows the radiation field and stays stable**

nodes.q: Her breathlessness could be pneumonia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, productive cough and lobar consolidation that clears with antibiotics**
**Afebrile with dry cough and persistent scar-like volume loss**

root.stem: An 8-year-old boy has had a painful lump in the front of his neck for 3 days after a sore throat. Examination shows a 3-cm, tender, rounded, cystic mass in the anterior midline, midway between the chin and the sternal notch. The mass moves up when he swallows and when he sticks out his tongue. There is no lump along the side of the neck and no skin opening.
root.oneliner: 8M + 3 days of painful anterior neck lump after a sore throat + 3-cm tender cystic midline mass + rises with swallowing and tongue protrusion + no lateral neck lump, no skin opening
highlight: tender, rounded, cystic mass in the anterior midline
moves up when he swallows and when he sticks out his tongue
no lump along the side of the neck and no skin opening

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The commonest congenital neck mass in children: a remnant of the thyroglossal duct that failed to atrophy. The clincher: **midline cystic mass at or below the hyoid that moves up with swallowing and tongue protrusion**.

nodes.q: From which point on the tongue did the thyroid begin its descent along this tract?
nodes.a: The foramen cecum at the base of the tongue
nodes.note: The thyroid forms at the foramen cecum and descends to the front of the neck along the thyroglossal duct, which normally atrophies by about weeks 8-10. Incomplete atrophy leaves a cyst; the tongue attachment is why the cyst rises with tongue protrusion.

nodes.q: Why did it become painful and tender after the sore throat?
nodes.note: Cysts often come to attention when they get infected; an old duct can drain to the skin as a fistula.

nodes.q: Where does the duct pass in relation to the hyoid bone?
nodes.a: Through (or just next to) the middle of the hyoid bone
nodes.note: This is why the hyoid has to be removed at surgery.

nodes.q: Which imaging test is done before surgery?
nodes.a: Neck ultrasound to show a normal thyroid gland in its usual place
nodes.note: The cyst may contain the only thyroid tissue the child has, so an ectopic gland must be excluded.

nodes.q: Which operation prevents recurrence?
nodes.a: Sistrunk procedure: removal of the cyst, the tract and the central hyoid bone
nodes.note: Simple cyst removal alone recurs often. Infection is treated first with antibiotics.

nodes.q: Which malignancy can rarely arise in the cyst?
nodes.note: Found in less than 1% of cysts; the removed specimen is examined.

nodes.q: A neck cyst in a child could be a branchial cleft cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lateral neck mass along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid; persistent second cleft; does not move with swallowing**
**Midline mass below the hyoid that rises with swallowing and tongue protrusion**

nodes.note: The trap: both are cystic neck masses in children that get infected.

nodes.q: His tender neck lump after a sore throat could be lymphadenitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tender nodes in the side of the neck, often several, that do not rise with swallowing**
**Single midline cystic mass that moves up with swallowing**

nodes.q: The thymus and inferior parathyroid glands also pass down through the front of the neck, so a third pharyngeal pouch defect could be offered instead. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Absent thymus and inferior parathyroids: low calcium with tetany and recurrent infections, as in DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion)**; no neck cyst
**Normal calcium and immunity; a midline cyst that moves with swallowing**

nodes.q: A firm midline neck lump in a child could be a dermoid cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Midline, often above the hyoid; does not rise with tongue protrusion**; contains skin and hair elements
**Rises with tongue protrusion and swallowing**, because the tract is tied to the tongue base and hyoid

root.stem: A 6-year-old boy who recently immigrated has had 2 weeks of unsteady gait and poor coordination. He has had a chronic cough since age 1 and is below the 3rd percentile for height and weight. His mother says his stools are bulky, greasy and foul-smelling, and his skin tastes salty when she kisses him. He has finger clubbing and rhonchi in both lungs. Neurologic examination shows a wide-based gait, absent ankle reflexes and loss of vibration sense. His red blood cells look normal on smear, his total cholesterol is normal, he has no scoliosis or heart murmur, and a gluten-free diet tried last year did not help.

highlight: below the 3rd percentile for height and weight
finger clubbing and rhonchi in both lungs
wide-based gait, absent ankle reflexes and loss of vibration sense
gluten-free diet tried last year did not help

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inherited disease of thick secretions. The clincher: **chronic lung infections + fatty stools and poor growth + salty sweat from infancy**, confirmed by a high sweat chloride.

nodes.q: Which gene is mutated?
nodes.a: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7
nodes.note: The most common mutation, delta F508, deletes a phenylalanine at position 508; the protein misfolds, is held in the endoplasmic reticulum and is degraded, so little reaches the cell surface.

nodes.q: How is it inherited?
nodes.note: Both parents are usually healthy carriers; each child has a 1 in 4 risk. Carrier rate is about 1 in 25 in people of northern European descent.

nodes.q: What does the CFTR protein normally do?
nodes.a: It is an ATP-gated chloride channel on epithelial cells
nodes.note: In the airways and pancreas, chloride is not secreted and sodium is over-absorbed, so water follows into the cells and secretions turn thick and dry. In sweat ducts chloride cannot be reabsorbed, so sodium stays too and sweat is salty.

nodes.q: Why are his stools bulky and greasy?
nodes.a: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency: thick secretions plug the pancreatic ducts
nodes.note: Lipase is missing, so fat is not digested (steatorrhea) and he does not grow.

nodes.q: Fat malabsorption leads to deficiency of which group of vitamins?
nodes.note: Treated with pancreatic enzyme capsules with meals and supplements of these vitamins.

nodes.q: Which one of them explains his unsteady gait and loss of vibration sense?
nodes.note: Lack of this antioxidant degenerates the spinocerebellar tracts and posterior columns; it can also cause hemolysis. Vitamin A lack causes night blindness, D lack rickets, K lack bleeding.

nodes.q: Which organism chronically infects the airways in older children and adults and speeds lung decline?
nodes.note: Mucoid strains make alginate. Staphylococcus aureus is more typical in infants. Repeated infection leads to bronchiectasis and clubbing.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Sweat chloride test (60 mmol/L or higher)
nodes.note: Newborn screening uses immunoreactive trypsinogen; genetic testing follows.

nodes.q: Which drug class corrects the faulty protein?
nodes.note: They help the protein fold, reach the membrane or open. Airway clearance and dornase alfa (breaks down DNA in sputum) help the secretions.

nodes.q: Which intestinal emergency can this disease cause in a newborn?
nodes.note: Thick meconium blocks the ileum; about 15% of babies with the disease present this way.

nodes.q: Which genital finding causes infertility in affected men?
nodes.a: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
nodes.note: Women have reduced fertility from thick cervical mucus.

nodes.q: His fat malabsorption and vitamin E lack could be abetalipoproteinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Acanthocytes (spiked red cells) on smear, very low cholesterol, absent apolipoprotein B-48 and B-100; retinitis pigmentosa**; no chronic lung disease
**Chronic cough with recurrent lung infections and salty sweat; normal red cells and cholesterol**

nodes.note: The trap: both give fatty stools, poor growth and vitamin E-deficiency ataxia.

nodes.q: His poor growth and fatty stools could be celiac disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, villous atrophy; improves on a gluten-free diet; no chronic lung disease**
**Chronic cough, salty skin, clubbing; no benefit from a gluten-free diet**

nodes.q: His ataxia and absent reflexes could be Friedreich ataxia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **GAA trinucleotide repeat in the frataxin gene; onset in late childhood or the teens with scoliosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes**; no malabsorption or lung disease
**Fatty stools and chronic lung disease from infancy; no scoliosis or murmur**

Chest x-ray shows reticulonodular infiltrates in both lower lobes and calcified plaques on the pleura, and microscopy of his sputum shows golden-brown beaded rods with a clear centre.

never worked in sandblasting, mining or the aerospace industry
reticulonodular infiltrates in both lower lobes
golden-brown beaded rods with a clear centre

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Interstitial lung fibrosis from inhaled asbestos fibers. The clincher: **lower-lobe fibrosis + ferruginous bodies + calcified pleural plaques after years of shipyard or insulation work**.

nodes.q: What are the golden-brown beaded rods in his sputum?
nodes.a: Ferruginous bodies: asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing protein

nodes.q: Which cell first engulfs the fibers and starts the fibrosis?
nodes.note: Long fibers cannot be cleared; the macrophages release growth factors and oxygen radicals.

nodes.q: Which growth factors from these cells drive the scarring?
nodes.a: Transforming growth factor-beta and platelet-derived growth factor, which activate fibroblasts
nodes.note: Collagen is deposited in the walls of the alveoli, starting at the bases.

nodes.q: Which pleural finding shows past exposure?
nodes.a: Calcified pleural plaques, usually on the diaphragm and sparing the costophrenic angles
nodes.note: Benign, and they do not turn into cancer by themselves.

nodes.q: Which cancer is the most frequent cancer in exposed people, especially smokers?
nodes.note: Smoking and asbestos multiply the risk; lung cancer is commoner than mesothelioma.

nodes.q: Which pleural cancer is specifically linked to asbestos?
nodes.note: Rare, often fatal; calretinin-positive; may follow decades after exposure.
